meta.source: Axiomate build log — defects and limitations found while building this application
meta.note: Every entry is a real occurrence during development. Closed items were fixed and verified in the build; open items are current limitations.

issues.subject: Editing any field destroyed a recorded closure date
issues.description: updateIssue rewrote actualEnd whenever status was present in the patch rather than when it had changed. The edit form submits the whole record, so fixing a typo overwrote a closure date recorded in the source log with today's date, silently. The guard now tests for an actual change, and the derived write is itself audited.

issues.subject: Auto-generated issue IDs collided with the imported log
issues.description: New issues were numbered from the workspace sequence, which also counts nodes and activities, so the first created issue was handed an id that already existed. nextIssueId now derives from the highest existing number for that client prefix.

issues.subject: Newly created structural rows were invisible
issues.description: visibleRows seeded its keep-set only from issue rows, so a Process Area or Engagement with nothing beneath it never rendered and could not be selected to add anything to. Empty structural rows are now kept deliberately.

issues.subject: Two dispatches in one tick silently discarded the first
issues.description: dispatch closes over state, so two synchronous calls both read the pre-change value and the second setState won. Latent until the assistant applied a change touching both fields and dates. dispatchMany now folds one apply chain and commits once.

issues.subject: Selection highlight did not apply to grid rows
issues.description: The rule used :where(), which has zero specificity, so the row background lost to the striping rule. Only found by looking at the screen — the code read as correct. Switched to :is().

issues.subject: Inline editor painted over the frozen columns
issues.description: The editing cell had a z-index above .sticky-col, so an open editor covered the frozen ID and Name columns while scrolled horizontally. Lowered, and ensureColumnVisible added for the Tab-advance path which had the same fault.

issues.subject: Grid lost every tab stop when the selection was filtered away
issues.description: Roving tabindex pointed at the selected row; when a filter removed it, no row carried tabindex 0 and the grid became unreachable by keyboard. It now falls back to the first visible row.

issues.subject: Committing an inline edit dropped focus to document body
issues.description: Both the commit and Escape paths unmounted the editor without returning focus, stranding keyboard users at the top of the document. Focus now returns to the originating row.

issues.subject: Escape did nothing inside dialog form fields
issues.description: The global handler bailed out on INPUT, SELECT and TEXTAREA before testing Escape — and dialogs open with focus in their first field, so Escape was dead exactly where it was needed. Escape is now checked first.

issues.subject: Evidence panel scrim painted beneath the focus editor
issues.description: An overlay opened from another overlay shared its layer, so its scrim rendered underneath and click-away dismissal silently stopped working. Added a stacked overlay token to the z-index scale.

issues.subject: Lifecycle checklist ticked with zero activities
issues.description: The claim "every activity has planned dates" showed a tick when no activities existed, because an empty list satisfies every(). It now requires at least one activity before the claim is made.

issues.subject: Reveal read pre-mutation state after applying a change
issues.description: revealIssue ran against the batched pre-setState tree, so a created issue appeared not to exist — raising a false "no longer in the workspace" error — and an updated issue was filter-tested on its old values, leaving it selected but hidden. It now takes the post-mutation tree.

issues.subject: Preamble text concatenated into the final answer
issues.description: Text from every tool-loop iteration was accumulated, so a narration sentence and the real answer arrived as one bubble — and were posted back as conversation history, compounding each turn. Only the turn that stops calling tools is kept.

issues.subject: Truncated answers were returned as if complete
issues.description: A response stopping at max_tokens carries no complete tool_use, so it fell out of the loop and was returned with no indication it had been cut off.

issues.subject: Search chips accumulated across every call in a turn
issues.description: Three narrowing searches produced roughly thirty chips, most of them rows the model had already discarded. Only the most recent round of hits is kept.

issues.subject: Apply guard let a double click through
issues.description: The claimed-card check read React state, which is stale within a tick, so two clicks both passed it. A second click on a create would have minted a second issue with nothing downstream to flag it as a duplicate. Moved to a ref.

issues.subject: Uncommitted term edits leaked across scope switches
issues.description: The terminology draft was keyed by label alone and never cleared when the scope changed, so text typed at organisation scope committed against whichever scope was selected when the field blurred. The editor now remounts per scope.

issues.subject: Assistant dock unmounted mid-conversation on selection change
issues.description: Dock visibility resolved autonomy against the selected row, so moving to a client with the agent switched off destroyed the open transcript. Visibility now resolves at organisation scope; only what a turn may do is scoped.

issues.subject: First configuration change of a session never saved
issues.description: The hydration flag was set inside a setState updater React can skip when the result is identical, so the save effect saw it false and skipped. Moving it to the effect body caused the opposite fault — the save ran before the loaded model was committed and overwrote storage with defaults. Both resolved by gating on state rather than a ref.

issues.subject: Malformed requests were reported as "no database configured"
issues.description: The endpoint checked for a database before validating the body, so a client bug produced the wrong diagnosis — and the entire validation layer was unreachable on any deployment without a database, which is the default mode.

issues.subject: Browser mirror overrode newly shipped structure
issues.description: The autosave mirror was returned whole rather than merged over the seed, so any record a later build adds was invisible forever to anyone who had used the app before. Caught when the Engagement tier failed to appear.

issues.subject: Prisma client constructed at module load broke the build
issues.description: Prisma 7 requires a driver adapter with a connection string, so importing the module without DATABASE_URL threw during next build page-data collection. Construction is now lazy behind a proxy, and running without a database stays supported.

issues.subject: Engagement and Project tiers rendered as Process Areas
issues.description: RowKind never carried them, so buildTree collapsed every non-client node to module and the Gantt group test missed them entirely. Added both kinds and a named isGroupRow so the next tier cannot silently render as an issue bar.

issues.subject: Name column truncated to uselessness at five tiers
issues.description: With Company and Engagement added, indentation plus rollup badges squeezed process area names to "Data Migr…". Badges now give way before the label, and the column default was widened.

issues.subject: Postgres read and write path has never been executed
issues.description: The schema validates, the client generates, the mapper round-trips in process and the no-database path is verified in the browser — but no working DATABASE_URL has been available, so the actual read and write against Postgres remains typecheck-only.
issues.nextAction: Supply a DATABASE_URL in .env, run npm run db:push, then create a Process Area and an issue, restart the server and create another to confirm no id collision.

issues.subject: Claude branch of the assistant has never been executed
issues.description: Without an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY every request answers through the deterministic parser, so the tool loop, the batch parse and the autonomy tool-withholding are typecheck-only.
issues.nextAction: Set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and confirm both the tool loop and that suggest-only autonomy withholds the proposal tools.

issues.subject: 37 of 38 registered agents have no implementation
issues.description: The registry records the decision for each agent — purpose, autonomy ceiling, whether a person approves — and exactly one, the Workspace Assistant, executes. The rest are marked declared and cannot be enabled.
issues.nextAction: Implement in priority order, starting with the P0 intake, classification and routing agents.

issues.subject: Routing rules and mail intake are configuration records only
issues.description: Both can be configured and are stored, but nothing reads a mailbox and nothing applies a rule: there is no mail connection and no scheduler in this build.
issues.nextAction: Requires a mail connector and a scheduler before the records have any effect.

issues.subject: Status and severity vocabularies are deliberately fixed
issues.description: They drive STATUS_PROGRESS and computeHealth, so a user-added value would produce issues with no progress and no schedule health. Making them configurable means making the derivation configurable too.
issues.nextAction: Model the derivation alongside the vocabulary if this is ever required.

issues.subject: No authentication: every action is attributed to one hardcoded actor
issues.description: Recorded when attribution and authentication were one item. They are separate problems and are now tracked separately, so this entry no longer describes anything on its own. The attribution half — a module constant read by the reducer at forty-seven sites, so every audited change in every workspace carried one hardcoded name — was fixed under AXM-043: the actor is a parameter, resolved on the server, with no field in the action for a client to forge. The authentication half, that nothing establishes who is making a request, is AXM-045 and remains open. Superseded rather than closed, because closing it would read as though authentication had been solved.

issues.subject: Schema was applied with db push rather than migrations
issues.description: There was no migration history, so an existing database could not be moved forward safely. A baseline migration is now generated from the schema and cross-checked against it: 10 tables, 7 enums, 18 indexes and 10 foreign keys, with no model unaccounted for. npm run db:migrate runs prisma migrate deploy. Not yet applied to a database, because none is reachable — and replaying a migrations directory to verify it needs a shadow database. Status is deliberately not Closed: the migration has been generated and cross-checked against the schema, but no database has ever been reachable here, so nobody has watched it apply. The prerequisite is AXM-025; when that is unblocked this closes with it.
issues.nextAction: Run npm run db:migrate against a real database to confirm the baseline applies cleanly, then use migrate dev for subsequent schema changes.

issues.subject: The source log carries no due dates
issues.description: committedDate, closedOn and committedOn are empty in all 179 imported rows, so every imported issue is Unscheduled until someone accepts an SLA proposal or records a date. A property of the data rather than a defect, recorded here so it is not rediscovered.
issues.nextAction: Accept the SLA proposals, or record real target dates per issue.

issues.subject: A docstring claimed read isolation the code did not provide
issues.description: persistActions documented that the load happened inside the transaction so two rapid actions could not build on the same snapshot. It did not — loadWorkspace ran on the client before the transaction opened. Found by review rather than by testing, because nothing observable was wrong until two writers overlapped. The claim and the code now agree.

issues.subject: Concurrent write batches could silently overwrite each other
issues.description: The write path loaded state, folded its actions and only then opened a transaction to write, so two overlapping batches both read the pre-change state and the second overwrote the first with no error and nothing in the audit trail to show it. The load now happens inside a Serializable transaction, and a serialization abort is retried up to three times so the loser replays against what the winner produced. Implemented but not yet exercised: no database has been reachable. Status is deliberately not Closed for the same reason as AXM-031: a serialization conflict has never actually been provoked here, and a concurrency fix asserted from reading the code is exactly the sort of claim this log exists to avoid. Blocked on AXM-025.
issues.nextAction: With a database available, issue two overlapping batches and confirm one serializes behind the other rather than being lost.

issues.subject: Three tier vocabularies described the same hierarchy and disagreed
issues.description: The delivery chain was enumerated in three places that had drifted apart. NodeKind listed five tiers; RowKind restated them plus three leaf kinds; a third list drove nothing at all, called the client tier "organization", and omitted company entirely. A fourth copy sat in the create/parent tables keyed by string, a fifth in the reducer as a four-way comparison, a sixth as a fallback label table, and a seventh in the CSS. Consolidated to one declaration, NODE_KINDS, with every other list derived from it and the third deleted rather than aliased. No string changed, so ids already stored in a browser or a database still parse.

issues.subject: Engagement rows accepted edits and drags for values that roll up from their children
issues.description: Two guards named only the Client and Process Area tiers, so once Engagement and Project became real tiers they fell through as if they carried work of their own. The grid offered inline Status and Severity editors on an Engagement row, and its Gantt bar was draggable — a drag dispatched setDates against a row whose dates are recomputed from its children, so the value was written and then discarded. Both now test membership against the tier list.

issues.subject: Company, Engagement and Project rows rendered as lifecycle activities
issues.description: The tree has four level treatments and the mapping named only client and module, so every other kind fell through to the activity style — muted, italic, 11.5px. Every workspace has a Company row and an Engagement row, so the two ends of the hierarchy were being drawn as if they were the smallest thing in it. Company and Client now take the banner treatment, Engagement, Project and Process Area the sub-group treatment.

issues.subject: An empty node created by the user was deleted from the local mirror on reload
issues.description: The mirror sweep removes seeded nodes a later build no longer defines, and identified them by matching the tier prefix of their id. User-created ids carry the same prefixes — a hand-made Engagement is engagement:47 — so any node the user added and had not yet put anything under matched the sweep, was absent from the seed, had no children, and was deleted on the next load with no message. Seeded ids embed what they name and user ids end in the workspace counter, so the sweep now excludes a numeric suffix. The tier list it matched on had also lost project.

issues.subject: The Type column shows the internal tier name, not the configured label
issues.description: Terminology is configurable and resolves down the scope chain, but the tree’s Type column rendered the tier name title-cased from a hardcoded union, so a workspace that renamed Process Area to Workstream still read "Module" there. It now renders the configured term, and a sub-issue shows the sub-issue term rather than being reported as an issue. The column resolves at the organisation default rather than at each row’s own scope, and the reason matters more than the change: the reducer already resolves there, so it is what every error message and audit entry says. Resolving per row would let the grid read "Workstream" for a record whose own History says "Process Area" — the grid and the trail disagreeing about one thing is worse than one term being less specific than it could be, and it would also break the column as a sort key by giving one kind several values. The app now has exactly two resolution policies: the reducer’s, at the organisation default, which the grid follows; and the ambient one that follows the selection, used by the Add menu and dialogs. A third would have been the same divergence the tier consolidation had just undone. Verified by renaming TIER_MODULE and confirming the column, the filter heading and the audit trail all followed.

issues.subject: The schema assumed one installation serves one firm
issues.description: Every application-supplied id was treated as globally unique, which is only true while there is one tenant: two firms both have a company:root, both mint rel-1, dep-1 and ev-1 from their own counter, and both may serve a client whose code is OAPIL. The configuration and the id counter were worse — each was literally a row with the primary key "singleton". Every table now carries a tenant, every primary key is (tenantId, id), every foreign key carries the tenant across so a record cannot be parented into another firm, and every uniqueness constraint and index is scoped by it. OperatingModel and WorkspaceMeta are keyed by tenant instead of by that literal, which also makes the import guard per tenant — a global seededAt would have refused to seed the second firm because the first had been seeded, and reported success while their tree sat empty. Done before the migration was applied rather than after, because this is the part that cannot be retrofitted without rewriting every key and every row.

issues.subject: The browser mirror was not namespaced, so two tenants would merge in one browser
issues.description: The workspace and the operating model were each stored under one fixed key. One machine that opened two firms would have merged their nodes, issues and configuration into a single workspace and written the result back as though it were one — the same shape as the seed-versus-mirror merge bug, with worse consequences. Both keys are now suffixed with the tenant. A mirror written before the rename would have been orphaned by it: the app would look under the new key, find nothing, fall back to the seed, and leave an afternoon of unsaved work on disk but invisible. It is adopted once instead, only by the configured tenant and only when that tenant has no mirror of its own, and the old copy is left in place as the last remaining fallback.

issues.subject: Tenant isolation is scoped but not enforced
issues.description: The data model is tenant-scoped and every query in lib/db names a tenant, checked by a script rather than asserted. What is missing is the thing that makes it a guarantee rather than a discipline: there is no identity in this application — no user, no session, no role binding — so nothing establishes which tenant a request belongs to. currentTenantId resolves one configured value and is the single seam where real resolution plugs in; the request body is never allowed a say, because a client-supplied tenant would look like isolation while being an open door. The enforcement layer is row-level security, which needs a database role per request, which needs identity. Recorded as open rather than closed with AXM-040 so the distinction between a scoped model and an isolated one stays visible.
issues.nextAction: Build identity first (Entra ID is the intended source), then resolve the tenant from the session in currentTenantId and add row-level security policies keyed on it.

issues.subject: Every audited change in every workspace was attributed to a hardcoded name
issues.description: The reducer read the acting user from a module-level constant at forty-seven sites, so the audit trail, and the raisedBy, createdBy, addedBy and updatedBy fields, all recorded one name that was compiled in rather than resolved. Two consequences, one worse than the other. The obvious one is that the trail asserted something it had not established. The subtle one is that apply() is the single funnel the server replays the client actions through, so the server produced the same hardcoded value and had no way to substitute its own — attribution could never have become trustworthy while the reducer was reading it from the air. The actor is a parameter now: apply(state, action, actor). Deliberately a parameter rather than a field of Action, because the browser sends the action and the server replays it verbatim — a field would be the client telling the server who it was, and there would be nothing to stop it. There is no field to forge, and what reaches the database is whatever the server resolved for that request. Proven rather than assumed: two actors applying one identical action produce two different audit entries, and the action object has no attribution field.

issues.subject: A viewer preference and a durable attribution were the same field
issues.description: SessionUser carried displayName alongside timeZone and locale, and the reducer attributed changes to a constant derived from it. So the string that decided how the header greeted you was also the string written permanently into the audit trail: changing how you wanted to be addressed would have rewritten who the system said had done things. Separated — SessionUser is viewer preferences only, an Actor is attribution, and the header now renders the actor so the chrome and the trail read one value instead of two copies of it.

issues.subject: There is no authentication, so no request can be tied to a person
issues.description: Attribution is now parameterised and server-authoritative, but nothing verifies anybody. There is no login, no session, no token, and no way to tell two people apart: currentActor() resolves one configured operator, which is honest for a single-operator deployment and is not identity. The consequence to keep in view is that this does not make the Permissions column of the capability matrix implementable. Authorisation needs a principal that has proved who it is; attribution only needs a name that was not invented, and that is the part that is done. It is also what AXM-042 is waiting on — tenant isolation cannot be enforced by row-level security until there is a database role per request, which needs a verified principal. Logged separately from AXM-043 so that a solved attribution problem is never read as a solved identity one.
issues.nextAction: Integrate Microsoft Entra ID: sign-in, session, and a User record per tenant, then resolve the actor from the session in currentActor() and bind roles to it. Unblocks AXM-042 and every Permissions cell.

issues.subject: Work type was free text, so 224 records could not be told apart
issues.description: The capability matrix asked whether work items should be one table with a type discriminator or ten separate tables, and called it the most expensive decision available. The data had already answered it: the imported records carry ten distinct types — 83 Defects, 48 Change Requests, 20 Queries, 19 Data Issues and six more — coexisting in one table with one schema and no strain. What was missing was that the model did not know. Type was free text with no registry, no filter facet, and it was not even in the search haystack, so searching "change request" matched nothing while forty-eight of them sat in the grid. It was also the one classification field the assistant could write without constraint, meaning a typo produced a record no filter would ever show. Work types are now configurable master data, seeded from what the records actually say they are rather than from the blueprint taxonomy — a registry pre-loaded with Risk and Decision would assert this firm tracks them, which the log does not show. Adding one is configuration, which is the thing that makes one table the right answer. Archiving one is refused while records still carry it.

issues.subject: The browser mirror took its operating model wholesale, bypassing the merge
issues.description: loadModel folds a stored model over the shipped one key by key, precisely so a model written before a key existed does not spread undefined over it. loadWorkspaceLocally did not: the mirror carries the whole workspace including its model, and that model was adopted verbatim. So on any browser that had ever run the app, a newly added part of the operating model arrived as undefined no matter how carefully the other path handled it — found immediately, because the new work-type registry rendered empty and the Archive list had nothing in it. The merge is now one exported function used by both paths. The same defect shape as the seeded-issues bug fixed earlier, one layer down: two ways in, only one of them merging.

issues.subject: The forms hardcoded the vocabularies the configuration screen edits
issues.description: Five literal lists sat in the two surfaces where records are actually classified: two work-type lists and three accountable-party lists, in the create dialog and the full issue editor. None read the operating model. So the accountable-party vocabulary was fully configurable — add and remove, with an editor and an audit trail — and adding one never made it selectable anywhere. The whole premise of the configuration plane, contradicted in the app’s own forms. The work-type list was also wrong on its own terms: it named nine of the ten types the workspace uses. Limitation was missing, so eleven existing records carried a type no form could produce, and no user could ever file another one. All five now read the model. Verified end to end: a type added in the configuration screen appears in the create form with no code change, which is the property the registry existed to provide and did not yet have.

issues.subject: Client log reclassified onto the blueprint work-item taxonomy
issues.description: The 179 imported OAPIL/SLG records were mapped from the nine types the support log recorded onto the blueprint taxonomy: Defect 49 and Change Request 48 map exactly; Query, Access Request and Estimate Request collapse to Request (37); Data Issue and Escalation collapse to Issue (35); Environment/Build becomes Task (6) and Status Chase becomes Action (4). The mapping is lossy and both sides are therefore kept. It lives in the transform rather than in a hand edit of the seed, so issues.raw.json still holds the recorded classification and re-running the transform reproduces the result. Every record also carries sourceType, and the record view shows it — "Issue - recorded in the log as Data Issue" — because after this nothing in type can tell an access request from a request for an estimate. An unmapped type throws rather than being guessed at, matching the rule already set for status.

issues.subject: The timeline left most of its pane blank at Month and Quarter zoom
issues.description: The scale multiplied a fixed pixels-per-day rate by the number of days in the domain, with no knowledge of how wide the pane was. That is correct while the domain is wider than the pane — Day and Week overflow and scroll — and wrong the moment it fits. This log spans about 118 days, so Quarter produced 177px of timeline inside a 667px pane: 56 per cent of it blank, every bar crushed into the left third, grid lines stopping in mid-air and the final column clipped to an 18px stub. Month was the same fault, less severe, with a 149px dead strip. Pixels-per-day is now clamped up to whatever fills the pane, measured with a ResizeObserver so it survives dragging the split and resizing the window. Day 3420px and Week 1364px still overflow and scroll unchanged; Month and Quarter now fill 667 of 667 with no dead strip. Where the domain is short the coarse levels converge, which is the honest outcome — once everything fits, zooming out has nothing left to reveal, and the header still changes granularity.

issues.subject: The filter bar wrapped onto a second row and split mid-controls
issues.description: Adding the work-type facet took the bar to eight, and the controls plus counts needed about 2150px against the 1432 available. It wrapped, and the wrap landed in a different place at every window width — at one size Schedule Health sat under the zoom buttons. Two changes. Each select now labels itself through its unset option ("Client: All") instead of carrying a separate uppercase caption, which the eight of them were spending more width on than the controls; and the four long or least-reached-for facets (23 process areas, 37 owners, severity, accountable party) moved into a More button that counts how many of them are set, so a filter can never be active somewhere the user cannot see it. Controls now hold one row with the counts on a status line beneath.

issues.subject: Completed work is hidden by default, with a toggle
issues.description: Of the records loaded here 73 of 229 are closed or superseded, so the resting view was largely history and the open work was scattered through it. Terminal records are now filtered out by default and the bar carries a Show completed toggle; nothing is dropped, and the counts strip reports "156 / 229 issues" so the hidden set is always visible. Two things this exposed. The active-filter test compared every value against the string All, which a boolean fails, so Clear would have looked permanently armed. And the done figure counted only visible rows, which reported "0 done" in a workspace with 73 finished — a summary reading as nothing has been completed because completed things are hidden. That one metric is now counted against the facets but not against the toggle.

issues.subject: Archive was a one-way door: nothing could restore a record
issues.description: The schema says records are archived and never destroyed, and every archive writes an audit entry stating it can be restored. Neither was true. The reducer arm existed and was allowlisted by the API, but nothing in the interface dispatched it, and every list filters deletedAt out — so an archived client, process area, issue, activity or evidence item left the application permanently, recoverable only by editing storage by hand. Two faults in the arm itself, both only findable once it was reachable. Archiving a branch stamps one timestamp across the subtree, and restore cleared the flag on a single record, so restoring the top of a cascade brought back an empty shell with everything inside it still archived. And restoring a record whose parent was still archived succeeded while producing something the tree can never reach, which reads as a restore that silently did nothing. Restore now refuses under an archived ancestor and names it, and otherwise revives everything sharing the target timestamp — precisely the cascade it belonged to, leaving records archived separately alone. An Archive panel lists what is archived, grouped by the action that archived it, and the entry point only appears when there is something to go back to.

issues.subject: Archiving with children moved up a level is not reversible
issues.description: Archiving offers two modes: take the branch, or take the record and move its children up one level. The second was not reversible — restoring returned an empty record while its former children stayed where they had been put. The cause was an audit gap rather than a missing field. Reparenting changed the parent of every child and wrote one line against the record being archived, and nothing at all against the records whose parent actually changed; their History showed no reason for having moved. Auditing each move — sharing the archive timestamp, exactly as the cascade shares deletedAt — both closes that hole and gives restore what it needs to reverse them. A record moved somewhere else since the archive is left alone: that was a decision of its own, and silently undoing it would be the same fault in the other direction. Entries aged out of the capped trail simply do not match, so the worst case is the previous behaviour rather than a wrong one.

issues.subject: The bottom panel became an issue workspace, not a read-only summary
issues.description: Overview was read-only with a full-page editor behind it, so the commonest action in a delivery tool — read a row, change one field, move on — cost a screen transition each way and lost the surrounding context both times. Overview now edits in place with explicit Edit, Save, Cancel and Discard actions, an unsaved-changes indicator, and a confirm before the selection moves to another issue. Deliberately not save-on-blur, which the rest of the panel uses: an explicit Save is what makes Cancel mean anything, and a twelve-field form that writes as you tab through it cannot be abandoned. Field edits and date changes are separate actions — dates carry scheduling validation and a reason — but Save folds them into one batch so a single press has a single outcome. Client and Process Area stay read-only against the brief, and the panel says why: they are not stored opinions but where the record sits, kept in step by the reducer on Move. A text box would let an issue claim OAPIL while living under SLG with nothing to notice.

issues.subject: Notes: the working record of how an issue actually progressed
issues.description: The panel answered what an issue is (Overview), what the system recorded changing (History) and what supports a claim (Evidence). None answered what was tried, what the client said, or why an approach was abandoned — which is most of what anyone needs when they pick an issue up three weeks later. Notes are a first-class entity: reducer actions, a tenant-scoped table with a composite key, soft delete, and a full audit entry per add, edit and delete. Reverse chronological with pinned first, ordered by last activity rather than creation so an edited note stays where its thinking is. Editing preserves the original author and time and records the editor separately, because a correction weeks later must not silently reassign who made the observation. Adding a note moves the issue lastActivity date — an issue whose staleness ignores three weeks of investigation notes reports the opposite of the truth. Kept out of the audit trail on purpose: an audit entry is produced by a change and nobody writes it, a note is written deliberately and describes what the system cannot observe. Merging them gives a trail too noisy to audit and notes that vanish when the audit cap trims.

issues.subject: Adding a note cleared the panel it was added to
issues.description: The new addNote arm returned createdId, which in this reducer means "a row appeared, select it" — and the workspace acts on it. So adding a note selected the note as though it were a tree row, found nothing, and emptied the detail panel the note had just been written into. Caught immediately in the browser rather than by typecheck, which had nothing to object to. A note is not a row and there is nothing to reveal, so the field is gone.

issues.subject: Editing permissions are a seam, not a mechanism
issues.description: The brief asked that editing and note-taking respect role-based permissions. What has been built is the seam: every editing affordance calls canEditIssue, canAddNote or canEditNote, so the day there are real answers the screens already ask the questions. What has not been built is any enforcement, and it cannot be yet — there is no authentication (AXM-045), so a permission model would be deciding what an unverified party may do, which reads as a boundary in every review while enforcing nothing. Three things are missing in order: authentication so a request has a verified principal; a role binding on it, since OrgRole and Person.roleIds exist but the seeded directory assigns no roles to anyone; and a role-to-permission map, of which there is currently no concept in the operating model. One real rule is applied already because it does not need identity to be worth having: a note may only be edited or deleted by the person recorded as writing it, since editing someone else’s account under their name misrepresents them. The check is weak while identity is unverified, but it fails closed and points the right way.
issues.nextAction: After AXM-045, add a role-to-permission map to the operating model and make the three permission functions consult it.

issues.subject: Daily IMS export
issues.description: Built. IMS is read as Issue Management Status — nothing in the source log expands it — and the report covers exactly the rows in view, filters included, printing that scope in its header rather than asking a question the screen has already answered. Two files come out together: plain text for pasting into an email or a call, and a CSV of the open rows for anyone who wants to sort them. Content is Position (open, severity, schedule health), Movement in the last day read from the audit trail, then only the sections that have anything in them — overdue, blocked, at risk, no owner, no next action, and open records quiet for a fortnight. Each is triaged most-severe-and-least-recently-touched first and capped at twelve, because forty-four blocked items printed in full turns a daily status into something nobody reads to the end; the CSV carries the rest. Two limits are printed in the report itself rather than left to be discovered. Movement comes from the audit trail, which is capped and — with no database — lives in one browser, so the report distinguishes "nothing recorded in this trail" from "nothing happened". And the imported log carries no due dates, so Overdue can only ever describe records scheduled in this app; against the real data it reads 0 overdue and 115 unscheduled, which is the truth about the source rather than a gap in the report.

issues.subject: Weekly client reporting export
issues.description: Requested: a weekly report for the client. Distinct from the daily IMS in audience rather than cadence, and that distinction is the whole design: a client-facing report must not leak internal notes, internal discussion, margin, effort variance or anything else the firm has not chosen to share. This is the first requirement in the system that needs a client-visible boundary, and there is none — no external user, no per-record visibility, no notion of what is publishable (a matrix gap already recorded). To settle: which client, per engagement or per client; what a client is entitled to see per record; whether notes appear at all and if so which note types; whether it reports progress against a baseline, and if so which one, given no baseline is stored.
issues.nextAction: Decide the client-visible boundary first — which fields and which note types a client may see. The report is a rendering of that decision.

issues.subject: Monthly governance reporting export
issues.description: Requested: a monthly governance report. The hardest of the three, because governance reporting is mostly about things this system does not yet hold: milestones, RAID, resource utilisation, SOW consumption, margin and delivery forecast are all named in the capability matrix as absent, and a governance pack assembled from what exists today would be an issue count wearing the title. What exists and is reportable now: issue throughput and ageing by client, engagement and process area; severity and status distribution; schedule health and blocked counts; and the audit trail as evidence of what changed and who changed it. What does not: anything commercial, anything about capacity, and any baseline to report variance against. To settle: who receives it and what decision it supports, which of the absent domains are prerequisites rather than nice-to-have, and whether an interim pack from the reportable set is useful or misleading.
issues.nextAction: Agree the audience and the decisions the pack supports, then confirm which absent domains (milestones, RAID, capacity, commercials) are prerequisites.

issues.subject: Due dates can be set from the SLA policy, in bulk and on the record
issues.description: The policy could suggest but never commit: a dashed bar on the timeline and a one-issue accept button. So the imported log had no due dates at all and every schedule-derived signal was inert — nothing was ever Overdue or At Risk, 115 open records read Unscheduled, and the daily IMS had a section that was structurally always empty. A derived value becoming a recorded one is the sharpest thing this codebase does, so it is deliberate at every step: the planner writes nothing, the preview leads with the consequence rather than the count, records that already carry a due date are never touched because a date somebody set is a commitment, and each date is written with the arithmetic that produced it — severity, working days allowed, and the raised date counted from — so a policy-derived due date can always be told apart from one set by hand. Applied to the workspace: 158 dates set (High 48, Medium 99, Low 11), 82 closed records skipped, none overwritten. 107 targets landed in the past, which is the correct answer rather than a fault — an issue raised in May with a five-day target and still open in August is overdue, and the only reason it did not say so was that nobody had written the target down. The counts went from 0 overdue / 0 at risk / 115 unscheduled to 69 overdue / 9 at risk / 0 unscheduled; the difference between 107 past targets and 69 overdue is the 44 blocked records, which report Blocked because that is the more actionable state.

issues.subject: The SLA policy was a frozen constant while it set real due dates
issues.description: The policy lived in useState with no setter — a constant in every practical sense — which was tolerable while it only drew a dashed suggestion on the timeline. Once it started writing real due dates, and therefore deciding what the daily report calls overdue, an uneditable policy meant shipping one firm’s numbers as everyone’s. Service levels are commercial terms, negotiated per engagement and different between firms; they belong in the operating model with the roles and the work types, not in the source. Now configuration: persisted, audited with before and after, validated in the reducer against whole numbers between 1 and 365 — a zero would make every record overdue on the day it was raised, and a negative or fractional value would put targets before the raise date. Reading it from the model rather than component state means editing it moves every proposal, every at-risk window and the daily report at once. The screen states the consequence that would otherwise be discovered by surprise: changing the numbers does not move dates already set, because a due date is a commitment somebody made rather than a live calculation, and it says how many records that currently affects.

issues.subject: Configuration had no index, so nothing said what was maintainable
issues.description: The screen opened on Terminology and offered a rail of nine sections. That answers where to click but not what is there: somebody arriving to correct a work type or a service level had to open every section to find which one owned it, and nothing anywhere stated what the operating model currently says. It now opens on an index — one card per area with its purpose and its live value, so "Service levels · High 5 / Medium 10 / Low 20" and "Agent registry · 1 of 38 implemented" answer most maintenance questions before anything is opened. Values are read on render rather than stored, because a maintenance screen reporting a stale figure is worse than one reporting none.

issues.subject: Nothing recorded how big a piece of work was, or how long it would take
issues.description: A record carried dates and a severity but no estimate, so the two questions every delivery conversation actually turns on — how much work is this, and when does it land — had no home except somebody’s memory. The Estimation tab answers both, and deliberately keeps them apart. Effort comes from five complexity parameters scored 1–5, which map through a centrally configured T-shirt calibration to story points and hours; the calibration lives in configuration because two firms running an identical complexity model will disagree about what an L costs, and the screen is forbidden from hardcoding it. Timeline is effort divided by capacity — hours per day, people, allocation — with the longest dependency chain as a floor beneath it, because steps that must follow one another take as long as they take no matter how many people are added. An earlier version of the arithmetic let four resources compress a strictly sequential week into 1.75 days; `npm run audit:estimation` now asserts that 1, 2, 4 and 8 resources all finish on the same day, and that independent work still divides. The tab states what it does not know rather than implying it does: capacity, waiting time and holidays are typed rather than derived, and estimated-versus-actual effort is absent because nothing in the product records hours.

issues.subject: Estimates lived only in the browser, so an agreed number could not survive a reload
issues.description: The estimation feature shipped through the reducer and the browser mirror but had no database behind it: no models, no mappers, nothing in the write path, and the two actions were not on the route allowlist — so a server replay would have rejected them and an estimate agreed on one machine was invisible on the next. `IssueEstimate` is keyed by the issue rather than an id of its own, because an issue has exactly one estimate and every screen arrives holding the issue. It stores inputs, not results: scores, capacity, steps. Total complexity, size, hours, duration and finish date are all recomputed on read, because each is a function of the T-shirt calibration, which is configuration and can change — storing the derived figures would freeze an estimate against a calibration nobody uses any more, the same rule that keeps duration and schedule health out of the schema. `EstimateRevision` snapshots both halves either side of a change, effort and duration, because they move independently: scope can grow without the date slipping if people are added, and the date can slip with no change in effort at all when a client goes quiet. Whether an edit amounted to a revision is decided once, in the reducer, and the write path persists that judgement rather than re-deriving it.

issues.subject: Nothing checked whether a business outcome actually happens end to end
issues.description: Every check in the repository asserted a mechanism: the reducer refuses an impossible date, attribution cannot be forged, archive reverses. None of them asked the question a delivery firm asks, which is whether the outcome happens at all — a screen, a button, a configuration record and a declared agent are evidence of intent, not of behaviour. `npm run validate:scenarios` drives 34 business scenarios through the real reducer and the real derivations and reports where each trace stops, using five verdicts because "missing" is not one thing: PASS, PARTIAL, FAIL, NOT TESTABLE, and NOT IMPLEMENTED. The distinction that matters is between PARTIAL and FAIL. PARTIAL means part of the trace works and the cell names the part that does not — an at-risk issue computes its health correctly and tells nobody. FAIL means the system does something and what it does is wrong or unguarded — an issue moves from Open to Closed in one step while seven workflow definitions sit in configuration that no code path consults. A NOT IMPLEMENTED verdict greps the source for the mechanism rather than asserting its absence, so the claim breaks loudly if somebody builds it and does not update the file. First run: 6 PASS, 13 PARTIAL, 6 FAIL, 7 NOT IMPLEMENTED, 2 NOT TESTABLE, with 8 findings at P0. Writing the harness also found four bugs in its own fixtures before it found anything in the product, which is the correct order.

issues.subject: The validation report is generated from the run, not written alongside it
issues.description: A report typed by hand can disagree with the run it describes, and the disagreement is invisible — the reader has no way to tell which is stale. `npm run validate:report` renders the page from `data/validation.json`, so every count, verdict, failure point and quoted measurement comes out of the run and only the surrounding prose is written. This is the same rule that keeps derived values out of the schema: the T-shirt size is recomputed from the score and the calibration rather than stored, because storing it freezes an answer against inputs that have moved on. A generated page also makes the harness worth extending — adding a scenario updates the report with no second edit, which is what makes it plausible that scenarios keep being added rather than the file rotting after the first pass. The rendered HTML is gitignored: it is output, and committing it would create a second copy free to drift from the first.

issues.subject: An issue could move from any status to any other in one step
issues.description: Open to Closed - confirmed, with no investigation, no client involvement, no evidence and no comment, was one click in the grid and the workspace accepted it silently. The product looked as though it had a lifecycle because it had one in two other senses — a plan of activities and a pipeline of agents — and neither governs the status field, so nothing did. The first validation run recorded this as workflow definitions that no code path consults; that was wrong in an interesting way, because those definitions are agent pipelines and were never a state machine. There was no transition model at all. There is now: a graph over the fixed status vocabulary, held in the operating model rather than in code, because the vocabulary is fixed (progress is derived from it) while the route through it is a delivery process that differs between firms. The rule worth arguing about is that Closed - confirmed is reachable only from Awaiting client confirmation: it is the only status whose name asserts something about the client, and reaching it directly means a consultant confirmed on the client’s behalf. Two requirements ride on the same object — a confirmed closure needs evidence on the record, and the two "we are not doing this" outcomes need a reason, which lands on the audit entry for the status field alone rather than on every field in the same save. Enforcement is itself configuration and defaults to on, because an unenforced default would reproduce the exact defect: configuration that describes a process and changes nothing. The graph governs changes, not history, so 600 imported records sitting in combinations it would never produce are not made read-only by a rule written afterwards. Every control that offers a status now offers only the reachable ones and says what is missing, because offering a value the reducer will refuse is worse than not offering it.

issues.subject: Every permission question returned yes, so no rule about who may do what could be stated
issues.description: The permission module was a seam that returned ALLOWED, and the reasoning was sound while it held: a permission model over an unverified principal is theatre, reading as a security boundary in every screen while enforcing nothing. It stops being sound once the rules themselves are the thing being got wrong. A firm could not state that a client user may raise work but not close it, that an analyst may triage but not agree an estimate, or that only an administrator may change the operating model — and validation could not test any of it, because there was nothing to test. Authorisation is now real: eighteen coarse permissions, a role-to-permission map in the operating model, and one check at the top of the reducer rather than twenty-odd scattered through its arms — a check per arm is twenty-odd chances to forget one, and a forgotten check is invisible because the action keeps working. The distinction the map makes that matters most is on the client side: client roles may raise work, comment and attach evidence, and may not close, schedule or estimate. A client confirming a resolution is a status the firm moves the record into on their word; letting the client move it themselves would make Closed - confirmed unfalsifiable. Enforcing this also exposed an older hole: note authorship had been checked in the panel since notes shipped and never in the reducer, so the rule held for people using the button and for nothing else that could dispatch an action. What is deliberately not claimed: authentication. Every request still resolves to one operator from an environment variable, so this stops a mistake rather than an attacker, and the fallback role — which ships as Administrator because a deployment with one operator and no login must still be usable — is where that honesty is concentrated. The screen says so in as many words, and the validation harness carries it as a separate open finding rather than letting the authorisation work absorb it.
issues.reference: lib/access.ts, lib/permissions.ts, lib/workspace.ts apply(), ConfigWorkspace Permissions

issues.subject: Nothing recorded hours, so five different figures could not be computed at all
issues.description: Actual effort, effort variance, cost, utilisation and how much of a fixed-price engagement had been consumed are all functions of one record that did not exist. The Estimation tab said so in as many words rather than showing a zero, which was the right answer while it held. Time entries exist now, and the entry is the record rather than the timesheet: a timesheet is a week of entries presented for approval, and treating the container as the record is exactly how an entry edited after approval silently changes an approved total. Hours are Decimal(5,2) in the schema, not Float — quarter hours summed across a month feed an invoice, and binary floating point cannot hold 0.25 three times over accurately enough to argue about with a client. Four things are refused: a day that has not happened, more than twelve hours in one entry, precision finer than a quarter hour, and logging in somebody else’s name without the grant for it. That last one is the same rule notes follow — hours are a person’s account of their own day — and a project manager who holds the grant may log on their behalf, with the entry keeping their name and the trail recording who typed it. Recording time also moves the issue’s activity date, because somebody spending four hours on an issue is activity on it. What this does not reach is money: cost needs a rate, and there is no rate anywhere in this application — not on a person, not on a role, not on an engagement. The tab says that too, rather than inventing a default hourly figure.
issues.reference: lib/time.ts, components/TimeTab.tsx, prisma TimeEntry, EstimationTab effort variance

issues.nextAction: SOW, so an approved change can move a value
issues.subject: A change request was closed by setting a status, which anyone could do
issues.description: Nothing distinguished an approved change from somebody marking it approved. Approval now exists as a mechanism with the three properties that separate it from a checkbox. It gates something: a rule names a transition, and the record cannot make that move until an approval exists and says yes — riding on the same transition graph the status field already goes through, so there is one answer to "may this record move" rather than two that can disagree. Not everybody can give it: a rule names the roles that may decide, and holding the general grant is not enough, so a project manager cannot approve a change the client sponsor is meant to. And not the person who asked: requesting and deciding are different acts by different people, and this is the one rule with no configuration switch, because a self-approval is not a weaker control but the absence of one. A firm wanting a shorter path widens the roles instead. Two further decisions. The question is copied from the rule onto the approval rather than referenced, so editing a rule later cannot rewrite what a person was actually asked — the same reasoning that makes an estimate revision keep its own before-and-after. And a rejection blocks exactly as a missing decision does and does not clear itself: somebody has to ask again, and the refusal stays where a reader can see the change was declined rather than never considered. The shipped rule gates a change request starting rather than finishing, because a change approved after delivery is a record of what was already done. Where it stops: approving a change does not move a commercial value, because there is no SOW to move.

issues.nextAction: A scheduled pass, for anything time-driven
issues.subject: Routing rules were records with no engine, so every configured rule was inert
issues.description: Nothing evaluated them and nothing could fail, which is not the same as working — and the configuration screen implied otherwise. There is now an engine, and the decision that makes it safe to switch on is that a rule acts by dispatching ordinary actions. It does not write to state: it produces the same Action values a person’s click produces, and those go through the same reducer, the same permission check, the same transition graph and the same audit trail. So a rule cannot do anything a person could not — it cannot close work with no evidence or move a record along a route the graph forbids, because the same code refuses it — everything it does is attributed with the rule that caused it, and a failure is partial and visible rather than silent and total, because each action is whole on its own. Events are derived by comparing the state before an action with the state after, rather than emitted by each reducer arm: an arm that forgets to emit is invisible, because the action still works. A comparison cannot forget, and an event is true by construction. Notifications are records with a delivery outcome rather than calls to a mail server, because the interesting question is not whether a message was composed but whether it arrived and whether anybody knows it did not. In-app is delivered because the inbox is the delivery; every other channel is recorded as pending, and the count of undelivered messages is shown to everybody rather than hidden behind a setting. What is deliberately absent is a schedule: every rule reacts to something that happened, so an issue going at-risk — which is time passing against a date nobody moved — has no event to subscribe to. That is now the honest reason the SLA watch stays declared, and it is a clock that is missing rather than a channel.

issues.nextAction: Rate, so consumption can be read in money as well as hours
issues.subject: Scope leakage was undetectable by construction, because nothing was contracted
issues.description: The statement of work was a text field on the engagement — a string naming a document nothing could be computed against — so there was no boundary for a request to be outside of, and the product could not do the thing a delivery firm most needs it for. A SOW is now a record under an engagement carrying a baseline: agreed effort and agreed value, both, because they answer different questions and move independently. A fixed-price piece of work can be on budget and badly over on effort, which is the case a firm needs to see before pricing the next one the same way. Against that baseline two figures are real rather than notional, because both of their sources now exist: planned consumption from the estimates on the work, and actual consumption from the recorded hours. The difference is scope position, and it is arithmetic. Attribution is by project rather than per record, following the domain model — a SOW sits between the engagement and the project, and work inherits it by where it lives. Per-record attribution would let two issues in one project belong to different contracts, which does not happen, and would make consumption a question with no reliable answer. Three refusals fell out of it: a draft SOW cannot have work delivered under it, a SOW cannot be archived while projects still point at it, and a project cannot be attributed to a SOW from another engagement. What the screen deliberately does not do is read a scope statement and pronounce on whether a request is inside it. That is a commercial judgement, and a machine answer would be wrong occasionally and confidently. It shows the consequence instead — agreed, planned, spent, left — and names the work its forecast could not see, because a forecast that treats unestimated records as zero is why a project looks fine until the week it does not.
